name: Chinese silk
blurb: The thread that gave the road its name, woven in the workshops of Hangzhou and Sichuan.

name: Porcelain
blurb: Celadon and white wares from the kilns of Fujian and Jiangxi.

name: Brick tea
blurb: Pressed tea, prized by Tibetans and steppe nomads.

name: Lacquerware
blurb: Carved red lacquer boxes and trays.

name: Ginger
blurb: Polo saw great quantities of ginger around Fuzhou.

name: Rhubarb root
blurb: Polo said the finest rhubarb grew in the mountains of Suzhou, sold across the world as medicine.

name: Musk
blurb: From the musk deer of Tibet. A small pod is worth a fortune.

name: Khotan jade
blurb: White and green jade from the rivers of Khotan, carried east to China for 2,000 years.

name: Samarkand paper
blurb: Samarkand learned papermaking from Chinese prisoners captured in 751.

name: Turkoman carpets
blurb: Polo called the carpets of Konya, Kayseri and Sivas "the finest and handsomest in the world".

name: Gold brocade
blurb: Nasij, cloth of gold woven for Mongol princes at Tabriz and Baghdad.

name: Muslin
blurb: Fine cotton cloth: the muslin of Mosul gave Europe the word, but the finest of all is woven in Bengal.

name: Glassware
blurb: Enamelled glass of Damascus and Aleppo, and Venetian glass shipped through Constantinople.

name: Damascus steel
blurb: Watered-steel swords, envied across Asia.

name: Rosewater
blurb: Distilled from Damask roses.

name: Olive oil
blurb: Pressed in the groves of the Aegean and Syria.

name: Flemish woollens
blurb: Fine European cloth brought east by Venetian and Genoese ships.

name: Red coral
blurb: Mediterranean coral, worn in Tibet and treasured in China.

name: Baltic amber
blurb: Brought down the Volga and through the Black Sea ports.

name: Sable furs
blurb: Furs from the northern forests, traded at the Golden Horde's markets.

name: Wax and honey
blurb: From the forests of the Rus principalities.

name: Lapis lazuli
blurb: The only great source of lapis in the world, ground for ultramarine pigment.

name: Balas rubies
blurb: Polo said the king of Badakhshan alone could mine them, on pain of death.

name: Turquoise
blurb: Mined at Nishapur and Kerman.

name: Saffron
blurb: Hand-picked crocus stamens from the Iranian plateau.

name: Indian pepper
blurb: Landed by ships from Malabar at Hormuz and Zaitun.

name: Frankincense
blurb: Resin from southern Arabia, burned in churches, mosques and temples.

name: Indigo
blurb: Indian dye, traded up the Gulf.

name: Dates
blurb: From the palm groves of Mesopotamia.

name: Dried fruit & nuts
blurb: Apricots, pistachios, almonds and the famous raisins of Turfan.

name: Wine
blurb: Georgian, Greek and Turfan wines, much loved at the Mongol courts.

name: Felt
blurb: Pressed wool, used for yurts and saddle blankets.

name: Caspian raw silk
blurb: Polo saw the silk of Ghel (Gilan) by the Caspian, and the silk weavers of Yazd.

name: Naphtha
blurb: Polo described a spring near Baku gushing oil "good for burning", carried away on camels.

name: Raw cotton
blurb: Cotton grows in every oasis of Transoxiana and Fergana.

name: Sal ammoniac
blurb: Collected from volcanic vents in the Tian Shan, used by dyers and doctors. A famous export of Kucha.

name: Jasper & chalcedony
blurb: Polo said the rivers of Cherchen carry jasper and chalcedony, sold in China.

name: Saddles & bridles
blurb: Fine leather tack from the horse peoples of the steppe.

name: Erzincan buckram
blurb: Polo praised the buckram cloth woven at Erzincan.

name: Gujarati cotton cloth
blurb: Printed and dyed cottons from Gujarat, the cloth that clothed half the Indian Ocean.

name: Pearls of Mannar
blurb: Polo watched divers bring up pearls off the Pandya coast, and saw the king wear 104 of them on a single cord.

name: Cinnamon
blurb: Bark from Sri Lanka and the far south, landed in the Pandya ports.

name: Cloves & nutmeg
blurb: From the Spice Islands far to the east, traded through the ports of the Malay peninsula.

name: Sandalwood
blurb: Fragrant wood from the hills of the Hoysala country, burned in temples from Cairo to Quinsai.

name: Ivory
blurb: Elephant tusks from the forests of Burma and Cambodia, carved in China into fans and seals.

name: Aloeswood (agar)
blurb: Resin-soaked heartwood worth more than its weight in silver. Champa's is said to be the best.

name: Malay tin
blurb: Tin from the river gravels of the peninsula, alloyed into bronze across Asia.

name: Cane sugar
blurb: Egyptian sugar refined in the mills of Fustat, and the raw sugar of Bengal.

name: Egyptian linen
blurb: Fine flax cloth of the Delta, prized since the pharaohs.

name: Balsam of Matariya
blurb: Grown only in one walled garden near Cairo. Christians believe the Holy Family rested there. Sultans send it as royal gifts.

name: Egyptian emeralds
blurb: From the ancient mines of the Eastern Desert, worked since Ptolemaic times.

name: Areca & betel
blurb: Chewed everywhere from Bengal to Vietnam, staining lips and teeth red.

name: Yemeni carnelian
blurb: Red agate (ʿaqīq) from the mines near Sanaa, carved into seals and rings.

name: Gold dust
blurb: Polo said the people of Zardandan covered their teeth in gold and paid for everything with it.

name: Salt cakes
blurb: In Caindu, Polo saw salt cakes stamped with the ruler's seal used as money.

name: Changthang wool
blurb: The fine underwool of Tibetan highland goats, carried down to the weavers of Kashmir and Persia.

name: Cowrie shells
blurb: Shells from the Maldives, used as small change in Bengal, and as money in Yunnan, Polo noted.
